title: Origami: Folding Paper into Art
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes without cutting or gluing it. The word comes from two Japanese words, ori, meaning folding, and kami, meaning paper. Although it is now thought of as a Japanese tradition, paper folding was practised in China and Europe too, and historians still disagree about where the first models were made. What is certain is that the craft became popular in Japan during the seventeenth century, when paper became cheap enough for ordinary families to buy.

Early origami served ceremonial purposes. At Shinto weddings, two paper butterflies were used to decorate bottles of rice wine, and folded paper strips called noshi were attached to gifts as a sign of good wishes. Samurai exchanged them too. Because paper was expensive and precious, these models were treated with respect, and the patterns were passed from parent to child by memory, not written down. The first printed book of instructions, published in 1797, showed how to fold the famous crane.

The crane has a special meaning for the Japanese. According to a popular belief, a person who folds a thousand paper cranes will be granted a wish, often for good health or long life. After the Second World War, a girl named Sadako Sasaki, who was ill after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, set out to fold a thousand cranes. Her story is told in a book read by children around the world, and every year thousands of paper cranes are sent to a monument in Hiroshima as a symbol of peace.

Modern origami began in the twentieth century with the work of Akira Yoshizawa, who invented a system of symbols, lines and arrows to show each fold. Before this, there was no common language for describing a model. His system, still in use, allows a folder in Brazil to follow instructions from a book written in Japan. Yoshizawa also invented wet-folding, in which the paper is dampened so that it can be shaped into curved forms that look more like living animals.

Origami has become a subject of serious mathematics. In the 1990s, mathematicians showed that certain rules govern every fold pattern, and that any shape with straight edges can in theory be made from a single square of paper. Engineers have since used these ideas to solve practical problems. A Japanese team designed a large solar panel that is folded flat for launch into space and then opens in orbit, and doctors have developed a tube for repairing blood vessels that is folded small to pass through a narrow artery before it opens.

Folding paper also has benefits for the mind. Teachers use origami in mathematics lessons to explain angles, symmetry and fractions, because pupils can see and touch each idea. Many of them report that children who fold models understand these ideas better. Dr Mei Lin Chan, an educational researcher, says that this is plausible, but she cautions that careful research is still needed before schools change their lessons, since pupils who enjoy folding may simply be the ones who were already good at mathematics.

For beginners, the best advice is to start simply. A square of paper, a flat table and a little patience are all that is needed. The first folds, the valley fold, in which the paper is folded towards you, and the mountain fold, in which it is folded away, are the basis of almost every model. Learners should crease each fold sharply with a fingernail, because a careless fold will spoil everything that follows. Many people find that, after the first few models, the craft becomes a relaxing way to end a long day.
